headline: The Stretch That Keeps Going: What Extreme EMA Extension Actually Predicts for the S&P 500
lede: When the S&P 500 races far above its medium-term moving averages, the instinct to sell — to wait for prices to "come back to earth" — is nearly universal. A statistical study covering 73 episodes since 1928 suggests that instinct has been costly.
body:
The chart making rounds in momentum-trading circles this week draws on nearly a century of S&P 500 data to examine what happens after the index stretches to uncommon distances above its 8-week and 21-week EMAs (exponential moving averages — smoothed trend lines that weight recent prices more heavily than older ones, making them quicker to reflect current conditions than a simple average). The threshold under study is not merely "a bit overbought": at 4.4% above the 8-week line and 5.5% above the 21-week, the index has entered territory that, by construction, has occurred only 73 times in roughly 95 years of data.

The headline finding is directionally clear and statistically stable: at a one-year horizon, the market resolved higher in 72 percent of those episodes, with a median gain of 13 percent. That figure climbs to 86 percent and a median of 12.6 percent when the sample is narrowed to the modern era — the 22 episodes from 2006 onward that cleared an even higher bar, representing the 90th-percentile stretch. Both numbers arrive with a sober caveat: the worst-case outcomes are severe. At the broadest sample, the one-year worst-case is a loss of 35.6 percent; even the modern cohort, which filters for particularly extreme extension, saw a worst one-year drawdown of 19.7 percent. The data is bullish on average, but it does not abolish tail risk.

The short-term picture is noisier and warrants more care. Over the first month following these episodes, median returns are barely above zero — plus 1.2 and 1.4 percent respectively — and win rates sit in the low-to-mid 60s. In the first week, the broader cohort's median is a flat 0.1 percent with only 53-percent odds of being positive. In other words, the data argues for patience rather than immediacy: the edge, such as it is, accrues mostly beyond the three-month mark. "Stretched does not equal doomed," as the study puts it, "but over one to three months, expect chop."

The poster, PurpleDrinkCapital — a market commentator with a growing following on X and Substack who specializes in long/short equities — frames this as evidence of a "Power Trend," a term coined by Investor's Business Daily and systematized by IBD's Mike Webster and Justin Nielsen building on William O'Neil's foundational work. A Power Trend is a precisely defined market condition, not mere enthusiasm: it requires that the index's daily low remain above the 21-day EMA for at least ten consecutive sessions, that the 21-day EMA itself trade above the 50-day simple moving average for at least five days, and that the 50-day SMA be rising. The signal must be confirmed on an up-day — IBD's principle being that exposure is never added during a declining session. The concept is distinct from casual observations of an "uptrending market"; it is a rules-based diagnostic indicating that institutional momentum is operating at high enough velocity to warrant maximum offensive positioning by trend-followers. Historically, the Nasdaq Composite has returned an annualized 18.1 percent during active Power Trend signals, against 5.4 percent when none was present.

The conceptual tension the data resolves — or tries to — is between momentum and mean reversion, two frameworks that generate opposite instructions when a market is "extended." The mean-reversion argument is intuitive: what goes up must come down; stretched rubber bands snap back; buy low, sell high. Academic finance, however, has repeatedly documented that this intuition misfires at intermediate time horizons. Narasimhan Jegadeesh and Sheridan Titman established in 1993 that portfolios of prior winners continue to outperform over the subsequent three to twelve months — a finding the authors revisited in 2023 and found still intact after three additional decades of out-of-sample data. The behavioral explanation centers on underreaction: institutional capital takes time to absorb and fully price a genuinely improved regime, so prices drift higher for longer than a simple reversion framework would predict. Extreme EMA extension, on this reading, is not evidence that the trend is exhausted but evidence that it is powerful.

The modern-era cohort amplifies this point in an interesting way. Its 90th-percentile threshold is more demanding, yet its one-year win rate is higher — 86 percent versus 72 — and its worst-case outcomes are less catastrophic. The intuitive explanation is selection: the modern episodes severe enough to crack the 90th percentile disproportionately occurred in the strongest bull-market regimes, when institutional flows, earnings revisions, and macro tailwinds were all aligned. Filtering for more extreme stretch inadvertently filtered for better-quality trends. The data does not specify where in any given cycle the current episode sits, and that is precisely the limitation the study's authors flag when they note that "every drawdown is real." The medium return is an average across episodes that included early-bull, mid-bull, and late-bull settings that look identical in the EMA-stretch metric but are very different in risk-adjusted terms.

concepts.definition: A rules-based market condition defined by Investor's Business Daily, requiring the index's daily low to remain above the 21-day EMA for at least 10 sessions, the 21-day EMA to trade above the 50-day SMA for at least 5 days, and the 50-day SMA to be rising — all confirmed on an up-day. It signals that institutional momentum is strong enough to warrant maximum offensive positioning in trending stocks.

A moving average that weights recent prices more heavily than older ones, making it more responsive to current price action than a simple moving average. The 8-week and 21-week EMAs used in this study track intermediate-term trend structure across roughly 2 months and 5 months of price history, respectively.

The percentage of historical episodes in a given lookback where the market was higher at the end of the measurement period. A win rate of 72% at 1-year means the index closed higher one year later in 72 of 100 comparable historical setups.

The tendency for extreme prices or valuations to revert toward a long-run average over time. As a trading framework it generates a sell signal when markets are stretched above trend; the EMA study presented here challenges this framework at intermediate time horizons.

A well-documented return premium in academic finance — first formalized by Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) — whereby past winners continue to outperform past losers over 3–12 month horizons, attributable to the gradual incorporation of information by institutional investors.

fact_check: The study's 73-episode figure and threshold levels (8w EMA ≥4.4%, 21w EMA ≥5.5%) are taken at face value from the original image as the underlying dataset is not publicly linked. The Jegadeesh-Titman momentum finding is well-documented academic literature. IBD Power Trend rules are verified from multiple public sources including Tradingsim and SentimenTrader. The Nasdaq Power Trend performance figures (18.1% vs 5.4% annualized) are sourced from SentimenTrader's published analysis.
